questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes the three components of Power BI?
options: Power BI Desktop is the free Windows app for connecting, cleaning, and building reports; the Power BI service is the cloud platform for publishing, sharing, and scheduling refresh; Power BI Mobile is for consuming reports and dashboards on a phone or tablet
Power BI Desktop and the Power BI service are two paid tiers of the same application, with Mobile as a free trial version
Power BI Desktop is cloud-based and the Power BI service is the installed Windows application
Power BI Mobile is where reports and dashboards are built; Desktop and the service are only for viewing them
The Power BI service is a free Windows application; Desktop and Mobile both require a paid license to even open
Power BI Desktop requires a paid license to connect to data; the Power BI service is free for all authoring
questions.explain: Desktop is the free, installed Windows application for connecting, cleaning, modeling, and building reports. The service (app.powerbi.com) is the cloud platform for publishing, sharing, and scheduling refresh. Mobile is for consuming reports and dashboards on a phone or tablet. Licensing costs only enter the picture once you share through the service.
questions.distractorExplain: Option C reverses the two: Desktop is the installed Windows application you build in, and the Power BI service is the cloud platform at app.powerbi.com you publish to and share from — not the other way around.

questions.prompt: A learner has been using Power BI Desktop to build and explore reports for weeks without paying anything. The first time licensing costs actually become relevant is when they...
options: share a report with colleagues through the Power BI service
open Power BI Desktop for the first time
load more than one table into a report
switch from Report view to Data view
questions.explain: Desktop is genuinely free and fully featured on its own. Licensing costs only enter the picture once you share through the service — Desktop and the service are not interchangeable, and nothing about building or exploring locally in Desktop requires a paid license.

questions.prompt: Put these five steps of the Power BI workflow in the order this course teaches them.
items: Get — connect to a data source
Transform — clean and reshape the data in Power Query
Model — relate tables and build DAX calculations
Visualize — turn the model into report visuals
Publish — share the finished report through the service
questions.explain: Every single thing you do in Power BI is one of these five steps, in this order: Get, Transform, Model, Visualize, Publish. Each step depends on the one before it — you can't model a relationship you haven't gotten yet, and you can't publish a report that doesn't exist.

questions.prompt: A learner connects Power BI to a plain .txt file containing lines of prose with no consistent comma, tab, or other separating character. What does the Text/CSV connector do with it?
options: Loads every line as one row under a single column, since no delimiter was detected
Refuses to connect, since Text/CSV requires a detectable delimiter
Automatically treats spaces as the delimiter, splitting every word into its own column
Shows the same Delimiter and Data Type Detection options as a comma-separated file, defaulted to Comma
questions.explain: The Text/CSV connector looks for a delimiter inside the file. When it finds none, there are no Delimiter or Data Type Detection options at all — every line simply becomes one row under a single text column named Column1.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Import mode and DirectQuery, per Chapter 2.
options: A DirectQuery table can be converted to Import, but an Import table can never be converted back to DirectQuery
DirectQuery copies data into the Power BI file, while Import leaves the data in the source and queries it live
Data volume in Import mode is limited by file size, while DirectQuery can handle much larger sources since nothing is copied in
Dual storage mode behaves as Import when that's faster and as DirectQuery when needed for consistency with a still-live fact table
Table (Data) view shows a DirectQuery table's cached rows the same way it shows an Import table's rows
questions.explain: Import copies data into the file (fast, limited by size); DirectQuery leaves data in the source and queries it live (handles larger volumes, speed depends on the source). You can convert a DirectQuery table to Import, but never the reverse. Dual mode is the hybrid behaving as either, depending on what a query needs. Table view shows cached data for Import and Dual tables, but shows nothing for DirectQuery, since nothing is stored locally to display.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: of the Web connector's five authentication types, ________ is the one built specifically for sites and APIs that authenticate with an API key.
questions.explain: Of Anonymous, Windows, Basic, Web API, and Organizational account, Web API is the authentication type built specifically for sites and APIs that authenticate with an API key — the one that matters most once you start working with real REST APIs.

questions.prompt: Match each term from the Get Data process to what it actually is.
right: Where you pick which tables/sheets to load, for any connector
A saved connection (source + settings, no data) that others can open to quickly build a new report against the same source
The short quick-access list on the Get data button itself
Where you can hand Power BI a hand-written SQL statement instead of browsing Navigator
questions.explain: Common data sources is the short quick-access list on the Get data button. Navigator is where you choose which tables/sheets to load, for every connector. A PBIDS file is a saved connection — source and settings, no data — others can reuse. Advanced options on the SQL Server dialog is where a native SQL statement bypasses Navigator entirely.

questions.prompt: A text column holding dates written as 22/01/2020, 23/01/2020, and so on throws DataFormat.Error when converted directly to the Date type. What's actually wrong, and what fixes it?
options: It's a locale mismatch — the dates are day/month/year but Power Query assumed month/day/year; fix it with "Change type with locale" and the correct region
The dates are stored as numbers instead of text, so they must be converted to Text first before they can become Date
Power Query can't parse any date containing a two-digit day above 12; the source data itself is corrupt
The column needs to be split by "/" into three separate columns before it can ever become a Date type
questions.explain: This is a locale mismatch, not a broken file: the dates were written day/month/year (UK convention), but Power Query assumed month/day/year based on the computer's region setting. Right-click the column, choose Change Type > Using Locale, and specify the correct region to fix every value at once.

questions.prompt: A query unpivots exactly the three date columns present today using plain Unpivot Columns. Next month, the source gains a new date column. What happens on the next refresh, and how could it have been avoided?
options: The new column is silently left out, because Unpivot Columns locked in the specific columns selected when the step was built; using Unpivot Other Columns instead would have picked it up automatically
The refresh fails with an error, because Power Query detects the query no longer matches its original shape
The new column is automatically unpivoted along with the rest, because Unpivot Columns always re-scans the source for every date-like column
Nothing changes, because Unpivot Columns and Unpivot Other Columns behave identically on refresh
questions.explain: Unpivot Columns locks in the specific columns selected the day the step was built, so a new column added later is silently left out. Unpivot Other Columns instead says "unpivot everything except [the columns to keep]" — it never needs to know the date columns' names in advance, so a new one gets picked up automatically on refresh.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Merge Queries vs. Append Queries, per Chapter 3.
options: Merge reaches sideways, pulling columns from one table into another based on a shared key; Append reaches downward, stacking rows from tables that share columns
Append matches columns by position, not by name, so columns must be in the identical order in every table being appended
A Left outer merge keeps every row from the left table, filling in null wherever the right table had no match
If one table being appended lacks a column the others have, the append fails with an error
An Inner join merge keeps only rows that matched in both tables
questions.explain: Merge combines columns sideways based on a shared key; Append stacks rows downward from tables sharing columns. A Left outer merge keeps every left-table row, null-filling unmatched right-side columns. An Inner merge keeps only rows that matched on both sides. Append matches columns by name, not position, and a missing column simply becomes null for those rows — it never causes an error.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a ________ is a named, reusable value you set once and reference in multiple query steps, instead of typing the same number or text directly into each one.
questions.explain: A parameter is a named, reusable value referenced across one or more queries. Change its Current Value once in Manage Parameters, and every step referencing it updates immediately — no hunting through Applied Steps to edit a hardcoded value in several places.

questions.prompt: Match each Power Query error-handling term to what it actually is.
right: Stops the entire query and shows a full-page yellow warning, usually from a missing column or an inaccessible source
An error in one cell that doesn't stop the query from loading
Drops every row where the selected column shows an error
Filters down to just the problem rows so they can be inspected separately
questions.explain: A cell-level error marks one cell without stopping the query from loading. A step-level error stops the whole query with a full-page warning. Remove Errors drops every row with an error in the selected column. Keep Errors filters down to just the problem rows for separate inspection, before deciding how to fix them.

questions.prompt: Put these Power Query performance habits in the order Lesson 23 recommends applying them, from how a query starts to where its most expensive step should end up.
items: Start from the purpose-built connector for the source, to unlock query folding
Set every column's correct data type before building anything else on top of it
Filter rows as early in the query as possible
Perform streaming operations like filters before expensive ones like sorts
Save an expensive operation like a sort for the end of the query
questions.explain: Starting from the right connector unlocks query folding. Setting correct data types early unlocks type-specific tools for every step after. Filtering early reduces how much data every later step has to process. Streaming operations like filters can return results as they read, so they belong before expensive operations like sorts, which must read the entire source first — exactly why a sort belongs at the end.

questions.prompt: After a Left outer merge on CountryID, one row's Country column shows null, even though the merge completed with no errors. What does that null actually indicate?
options: That row's CountryID had no matching row in the right-hand Countries table — the merge is working correctly and surfacing a genuine gap in the reference table
The merge itself failed for that one row only, while succeeding for every other row
Power Query always fills the last row of a merged column with null as a placeholder
The Countries table has too many columns, so Power Query truncated the extra ones to null
questions.explain: A Left outer merge keeps every row from the left table, matched or not. A null in the new column means that row's key had no match on the right side — it's informative, not an error, and it tells you the reference table is missing a row.

questions.prompt: A Conditional Column has three clauses: If CustomerGroup equals 1 Then Tier 1 Price, Else if CustomerGroup equals 2 Then Tier 2 Price, Else Tier 3 Price. For a row where CustomerGroup equals 2, which value does Final Price show?
options: Tier 2 Price, because conditions are tested top to bottom and the first match wins
Tier 3 Price, because the Else clause always overrides earlier matches
All three tier prices added together
Tier 1 Price, because the first clause is always evaluated last and takes priority
questions.explain: Conditional Column clauses are tested top to bottom, and the first match wins. For CustomerGroup = 2, the first clause (equals 1) fails, the second clause (equals 2) matches, so Final Price shows Tier 2 Price — the Else clause never runs once an earlier condition matched.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes star schema, as Power BI's recommended data model design?
options: One fact table sits at the center, with dimension tables connected directly to it, each by its own relationship — giving every dimension exactly one path to reach the fact table
Every table in the model must be a dimension table; fact tables are an outdated design Power BI no longer recommends
Star schema requires splitting every dimension across multiple related tables, so each level of a hierarchy lives in its own table
A star schema connects every table directly to every other table, maximizing the number of relationships in the model
Star schema means dimension tables sit at the center, summarizing data, surrounded by fact tables that filter and group them
Star schema is only a visual arrangement in Model view, with no effect on how Power BI's query engine actually processes filters
questions.explain: Star schema puts one fact table at the center, with dimension tables connected directly to it, each by its own relationship. This gives every dimension exactly one, unambiguous path to the fact table, which is exactly what makes Power BI's query engine's job predictable.
questions.distractorExplain: Option C describes a snowflake, not a star — splitting a dimension's levels across multiple related tables (like Category, Subcategory, and Product in three separate tables) loses the ability to build one hierarchy spanning both, which is the opposite of what star schema is designed to preserve.

questions.prompt: A report builds a table visual with a Priority column from one table and a summed Hours column from a second, completely unrelated table. Every row shows the exact same total instead of different values per priority. Why?
options: There's no relationship connecting the two tables, so Power BI has no way to know which hours belong to which priority — it just repeats the grand total
The Hours column needs to be converted to a measure before it can be filtered by Priority
Priority needs to be set to the Whole Number data type instead of Text
The visual needs a slicer added before cross-filtering will work between unrelated tables
questions.explain: Without a relationship, Power BI has no path connecting the two tables, so it can't tell which hours belong to which priority — every row just repeats the unfiltered grand total. Creating the correct relationship (autodetect or manually) fixes this immediately, with no change needed to the visual itself.

questions.prompt: A model has a sales-actuals table and a budget table, both related to the same department lookup table. Setting cross filter direction to Both on every relationship causes Power BI to reject part of the model. Why?
options: The shared lookup table creates a loop — with Both set everywhere, a filter has more than one path to reach the same table, and Power BI can't resolve the ambiguity
Both direction is only valid on relationships to a date table, never to any other lookup table
Power BI silently ignores the setting and defaults back to Single with no warning
Many-to-many relationships are never allowed in a Power BI model, regardless of filter direction
questions.explain: Two fact-like tables sharing one lookup table form a loop — a table reachable from another by more than one path. Setting Both everywhere gives a filter more than one route to travel, and Power BI can't pick one for you, so it blocks the relationship rather than guess. Marking one relationship inactive, or duplicating the shared table under two names, fixes it.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about active and inactive relationships, per Chapter 4.
options: Power BI allows only one active relationship between any two tables at a time
An inactive relationship is deleted from the model and must be rebuilt before it can ever be used
A DAX measure can reach an inactive relationship for one calculation using USERELATIONSHIP
Checking a different relationship as active in Manage relationships automatically unchecks the one that was previously active between those same two tables
Role-playing dimensions (like Order/Due/Ship Date all pointing at one Date table) require three separate Date tables, one per role
questions.explain: Only one relationship between any two tables can be active at once. An inactive relationship isn't deleted — it's dormant, reachable by a measure via USERELATIONSHIP. Checking a different relationship as active unchecks the previous one, since only one checkbox can be active at a time. Role-playing dimensions use one Date table with multiple relationships to the same fact table, not three separate Date tables.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a fact table's ________ is the level of detail one row represents — for example, one row per sale, versus one row per product per month.
questions.explain: Granularity is the level of detail one fact table row represents. Two dimension key columns don't tell you the granularity by themselves — you have to check what values those keys actually hold to know what a SUM or COUNT against that table is really adding up.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes what the DAX CALCULATE function does?
options: It evaluates an expression inside a modified filter context, using its filter arguments to narrow or change what the expression sees
It converts a calculated column's row context permanently into a filter context for every future calculation in the model
It is an iterator function that evaluates its expression once per row of a table and sums the results
It only works when passed a table expression built with FILTER — a Boolean condition isn't a valid argument
It replaces SUM, AVERAGE, and COUNT as DAX's only aggregation function
It permanently changes a column's stored values, the same way a calculated column does
questions.explain: CALCULATE evaluates an expression — almost always a measure or an aggregation — inside a filter context modified by its filter arguments. Called with no filters, it behaves exactly like the expression alone; the filters are where the power is, and nearly everything advanced in DAX is built on top of this one function.
questions.distractorExplain: Option C describes SUMX and the rest of the iterator (X-suffixed) family, not CALCULATE. CALCULATE doesn't walk a table row by row — it modifies the filter context that an aggregation function like SUM or an iterator like SUMX is then evaluated against.

questions.prompt: This formula lives in a calculated column. What determines which Region's TaxRate gets pulled in for each row?
options: Row context — RELATED follows the relationship from the current row to the related Region table and pulls that row's TaxRate
Filter context from whatever slicers happen to be on the report when the column was created
The alphabetically first TaxRate value in the Region table, applied to every row
CALCULATE, which is implicitly wrapped around every calculated column formula
questions.explain: A calculated column is evaluated once per row, in row context — DAX knows which row it's currently on with no filter or WHERE clause involved. RELATED extends that row context across a relationship, pulling in the TaxRate tied to the current row's region specifically.

questions.prompt: A report already has a slicer on Product[Color] set to "Red". What does the Blue Revenue measure show?
options: Blue-only revenue, because CALCULATE's filter argument overwrites the existing filter on that same column rather than combining with it
Zero, because the slicer's Red filter and CALCULATE's Blue filter cancel each other out
Revenue for both Red and Blue combined, because CALCULATE's filter adds to the slicer's filter
Red-only revenue, because the report-level slicer always takes priority over a measure's own CALCULATE filter
questions.explain: When CALCULATE's filter argument targets a column that's already filtered, it overwrites the existing filter by default rather than combining with it. The measure forces its own Blue condition on top of whatever the slicer selected, so it always shows Blue-only revenue regardless of the slicer.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about SUM, COUNT, COUNTA, COUNTROWS, and DISTINCTCOUNT, per Chapter 5.
options: COUNT only counts rows with a non-blank numeric value — it returns 0 on a text column
COUNTROWS counts table rows directly, ignoring column content entirely
DISTINCTCOUNT category-level totals always add up exactly to the DISTINCTCOUNT grand total
COUNTA counts any non-blank value regardless of type — numbers, text, or dates
SUM, AVERAGE, MIN, and MAX all skip NULL values rather than treating them as zero
questions.explain: COUNT counts only non-blank numeric values, returning 0 on a text column. COUNTROWS counts rows directly, ignoring content. COUNTA counts any non-blank value regardless of type. SUM, AVERAGE, MIN, and MAX all skip NULLs rather than treating them as zero. DISTINCTCOUNT is non-additive — its grand total can be smaller than the sum of its category-level values, since a row counted in two categories is still only one distinct value overall.

questions.prompt: Why does this measure need SUMX instead of a plain SUM?
options: The value being summed — Quantity times UnitPrice — doesn't exist as a single stored column, so it has to be calculated fresh for every row before it can be summed
SUM can't be used on any column that contains decimal values
SUMX is required whenever a measure references more than one table
SUM would return the wrong data type, while SUMX always returns a whole number
questions.explain: SUM aggregates one existing column directly — but there's no single stored column holding Quantity times UnitPrice. SUMX iterates row by row, evaluates that expression fresh for each row, and sums the results — exactly the case where a plain aggregation function can't do the job.

questions.code:
Customer Segment =
IF (
    CALCULATE ( SUM ( Sales[Sales Amount] ), ALLEXCEPT ( Customer, Customer[CustomerKey] ) ) < 2500,
    "Low", "High"
)
questions.prompt: This formula is a calculated column on the Customer table. How can CALCULATE inside it possibly depend on filtering the separate Sales table, given that a calculated column only ever sees row context?
options: CALCULATE triggers context transition: the current row's CustomerKey becomes a one-row filter context, which — through the relationship to Sales — restricts SUM to just that customer's sales
It can't actually work this way; the formula silently returns the same value for every customer
ALLEXCEPT converts the entire Customer table into row context before CALCULATE ever runs
RELATED is implicitly added by Power BI any time CALCULATE appears inside a calculated column
questions.explain: CALCULATE evaluated inside row context triggers context transition: the current row (one customer's CustomerKey) becomes a filter context as if the whole model were filtered to just that customer. ALLEXCEPT then clears any other filters on Customer while keeping that one, so SUM sums only that customer's sales through the relationship to the Sales table.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: unlike the plain / operator, which throws an error on a zero denominator, DIVIDE(<numerator>, <denominator>) returns ________ instead, unless you specify an alternate result.
questions.explain: DIVIDE returns blank (or a value you specify as a third argument) instead of erroring when the denominator is zero or blank — exactly the kind of jarring error a report-facing formula should avoid, which is why DIVIDE should be the default over plain / in report measures.

questions.prompt: Match each DAX filter-clearing function to what it actually does.
right: Removes every filter created by the visual's own row/column layout, but keeps slicers and report-level filters
Removes every filter on a table except the named column(s)
Clears filters from specified tables/columns, or everywhere if called with no arguments — purpose-built only for clearing
Removes every filter from the specified table, ignoring whatever's currently active
questions.explain: ALL(Table) removes every filter on that table outright. ALLEXCEPT(Table, Column) removes every filter except the named columns. ALLSELECTED() keeps report-level and slicer filters, removing only what the visual's own layout added. REMOVEFILTERS() clears filters from named columns/tables (or everywhere), and unlike ALL it can only clear — it never also returns a table the way ALL can.

questions.prompt: A report is already filtered to Washington and British Columbia via a slicer. What does this measure show?
options: Washington only — KEEPFILTERS makes the new filter intersect with the existing slicer filter instead of overwriting it, and WA is the only state in both
Washington, Oregon, and British Columbia combined, because KEEPFILTERS unions the two filters together
Oregon only, because KEEPFILTERS always keeps the measure's own filter and discards the slicer
An error, because KEEPFILTERS can't be combined with an OR condition inside CALCULATE
questions.explain: KEEPFILTERS changes CALCULATE's default overwrite behavior so the new filter combines with (intersects) the existing one instead of replacing it. The slicer already narrowed to WA and BC; the measure's filter narrows to WA and OR. The only state in both sets is Washington, so that's what the result shows.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of using VAR/RETURN to debug a DAX formula in the correct order.
items: Write the formula with VAR defining the subexpression to inspect
Comment out the real RETURN expression while testing
Change the RETURN line to temporarily output just that variable
Check the value the formula now returns for that variable alone
Restore the real RETURN expression once the variable's value is confirmed correct
questions.explain: Write the formula with the suspect subexpression captured in a VAR, temporarily comment out the real RETURN line, swap in a RETURN that outputs just that variable, check the number it produces, then restore the real RETURN once you've confirmed the variable holds the value you expected — a fast way to isolate exactly which part of a formula is misbehaving.

questions.prompt: A table has one row per day except for a single missing day in March, where no row exists at all. Power BI rejects it when you try to mark it as a date table. Which validation rule did it fail?
options: Contiguous dates — there's a gap, since not every day between the first and last date exists as a row
Unique values — the missing day means a duplicate date exists somewhere else
No null values — a missing row always means a null date value
Consistent timestamp — a missing row changes the time portion of every other row
questions.explain: Power BI's four date-table validation rules are unique values, no nulls, contiguous dates, and (if a Date/Time column) a consistent timestamp. A single missing day breaks contiguity specifically — there's a gap between the first and last date, which is exactly what this rule checks for.

questions.prompt: Why does this formula use DATEADD with YEAR instead of simply subtracting 365 days from every date?
options: DATEADD understands calendar units, so shifting back one year correctly lands on the same month and day the following year regardless of leap years — a fixed 365-day shift wouldn't
Subtracting 365 days is syntactically invalid inside CALCULATE
DATEADD is faster to calculate than any arithmetic performed directly on a date column
A fixed day count can never be used as a filter argument to CALCULATE
questions.explain: DATEADD shifts by calendar units, not a fixed day count — shifting back one year correctly lands on the same month and day a year earlier regardless of leap years, and shifting by a month correctly handles months of different lengths. A flat 365-day subtraction would drift off by a day across a leap year.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: TOTALYTD(<expr>, <dates>) is exactly equivalent to CALCULATE(<expr>, ________(<dates>)) — TOTALYTD just saves the extra typing for the most common case.
questions.explain: TOTALYTD is shorthand for CALCULATE combined with DATESYTD. Writing DATESYTD explicitly matters once you need to combine the year-to-date restriction with other filter arguments in the same CALCULATE call, since TOTALYTD only accepts a single additional filter.

questions.prompt: A matrix's default total row sums a sales column across the full filter context of the page, but the report actually needs that total row to show the average instead. What's the right way to change it?
options: Right-click the numeric column and choose "Customize total calculation" to set it to Average
Rebuild the entire matrix as two separate table visuals
Change the underlying measure's DAX from SUM to AVERAGE, which changes every other use of it too
Totals can't be customized — only the detail rows can be changed
questions.explain: Right-clicking a numeric column in a matrix and selecting "Customize total calculation" lets you override what that one total row displays — sum, average, min, max, distinct count, count, or none — without touching the underlying measure or rebuilding the visual.

questions.prompt: A report builder tries to set a scatter chart to cross-highlight (rather than cross-filter) another visual on the page, but the option isn't available. Why?
options: Line charts, scatter charts, and maps can only be cross-filtered, never cross-highlighted — a limitation of those visual types
Cross-highlighting was removed from Power BI and replaced entirely by cross-filtering
Edit interactions must be turned on before Highlight becomes selectable, regardless of visual type
Scatter charts can only interact with other scatter charts
questions.explain: Line charts, scatter charts, and maps can only be cross-filtered, never cross-highlighted — this is a built-in limitation of those specific visual types, not a setting that can be toggled around.

questions.prompt: A slicer has "Show 'Select all' option" turned on. A viewer selects Select all, then clears one value ("Small Business"). Select every true statement about what happens.
options: Power BI applies an "is not" filter containing only the cleared value, not an "is" filter listing every remaining value
Selecting Select all with nothing then cleared applies no filter at all, the same as clearing every selection
A new value added to the source during a future refresh will automatically be included, since nothing explicitly excludes it
The slicer behaves identically to manually checking every value except Small Business
Clearing one value after Select all always resets the slicer back to no selections
questions.explain: Select all with nothing cleared applies no filter, same as clearing every selection. Clearing one value afterward applies an "is not" filter on just that value, not an "is" filter listing everything else. That matters because a brand-new value added later is automatically included, since nothing explicitly excludes it — unlike manually checking every current value, which wouldn't show a new value until the selection is updated by hand.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: both Forecasting and Anomaly detection, in the Analytics pane, are available only on ________ charts.
questions.explain: Forecasting and Anomaly detection are both line-chart-only features in the Analytics pane. Forecasting needs a genuine time axis to project from, and anomaly detection needs the same continuous trend to flag unexpected spikes or dips against.

questions.prompt: Match each report-navigation term to what it actually does.
right: Moves through hierarchy levels within a single visual
Navigates to a separate report page, pre-filtered to whatever was selected
Saves a page's filters, selections, and visibility state so it can be reapplied with one click
Shows per-visual Filter/Highlight/None controls for how a selected visual affects the rest of the page
questions.explain: Drill mode moves through hierarchy levels inside one visual. Drillthrough navigates to a separate page, pre-filtered to the selection. A bookmark saves a page's full state — filters, selections, visibility — for one-click recall. Edit interactions shows the per-visual Filter/Highlight/None controls governing how a selected visual affects the rest of the page.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of building and using a drillthrough page in the correct order.
items: Add a new report page and rename it to describe its purpose
Drag a field into the Drillthrough filters well in the Visualizations pane
Add visuals to the page that make sense at the individual-item level
Right-click a data point on a visual containing that same field and select Drillthrough
Select Back on the automatically-added button to return to the summary page
questions.explain: A drillthrough page starts as a new, renamed page, gets a field dropped into the Drillthrough filters well, and is then populated with visuals suited to that one item's detail. Only after that setup does right-clicking a matching data point elsewhere surface the Drillthrough option, and the automatically-added Back button returns to where you started.

questions.prompt: A proposed dashboard tile shows "Total Revenue: $2.3M" with no comparison of any kind. Per Chapter 8, why doesn't this yet qualify as a genuine KPI?
options: A KPI needs a target or benchmark to compare against — a raw value on its own doesn't tell anyone whether $2.3M is good or bad
KPIs must always be displayed as a percentage, never a dollar figure
A number only becomes a KPI once it's shown in a card visual specifically
Total Revenue can never be a KPI, regardless of context, because it isn't actionable
questions.explain: A genuine KPI compares its value against something — a target, a prior period, a benchmark. A raw number with nothing to compare against is a candidate for a plain card, not a KPI visual, which exists specifically to show progress toward a defined goal.

questions.prompt: Select every chart choice Chapter 8 identifies as a genuine distortion — one that misrepresents the underlying comparison.
options: A column chart whose Y-axis doesn't start at zero
A 3D pie chart
A combo chart using a second axis to show a measure in the thousands alongside one in the millions
A pie chart with eleven categories, compared by slice angle
Sorting a bar chart by measure value to draw attention to the highest performer
questions.explain: A truncated (non-zero) axis and 3D effects both distort the visual comparison between values. A pie chart past roughly eight categories asks the eye to compare angles it can't reliably judge. A second axis on a combo chart is the honest fix for mismatched scales, not a distortion — and sorting by measure value is a deliberate, honest storytelling choice, not a trick.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: most audiences read a dashboard ________ to bottom, left to right — which is exactly why the single most important number belongs in the top-left corner.
questions.explain: Most audiences read top to bottom, left to right. That single fact drives the layout advice to put the highest-level information in the top-left corner, so a viewer grasps the headline before they've consciously started reading the rest of the page.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes what happens when you publish a .pbix file to the Power BI service?
options: Publishing sends the semantic model (tables, relationships, measures) and any report pages to the service; the underlying Power Query steps stay editable only in Desktop
Publishing uploads only the report's visuals as static images, with no live semantic model behind them
Publishing automatically creates a new workspace for the file if one doesn't already exist
Publishing permanently deletes the original .pbix file from the local machine once the upload succeeds
Changes made to a report inside the service are automatically written back to the original .pbix file the next time Desktop opens it
Publishing converts an Import-mode semantic model to DirectQuery automatically, to keep the service copy current
questions.explain: Publishing sends the semantic model (tables, relationships, measures) and any Report-view pages to the service. The Power Query steps that built that model stay editable only in Desktop — they never travel to the service as separate, editable objects.
questions.distractorExplain: Option E is the mistake this chapter specifically warns against: a change made to a report inside the service never writes back to the original .pbix file. The two copies diverge the moment you publish, which is exactly why republishing (not editing in the service) is how Desktop changes reach the service.

questions.prompt: A Pro-licensed report builder wants to share a dashboard with a colleague who only has a Free license. Under what condition can that colleague actually view it?
options: Only if the dashboard's workspace is assigned to a Premium or Fabric capacity — a Free user can't view shared content in an ordinary shared-capacity workspace
Any Pro user can always share with any Free user, regardless of where the workspace lives
The Free user would first need to be upgraded to Premium Per User, which removes the restriction entirely
Sharing with a Free-license user is never possible under any circumstance
questions.explain: A Free license alone can't view shared content in an ordinary shared-capacity workspace. Content stored in a workspace assigned to a Premium or Fabric capacity behaves differently: a Pro user can share it with a Free-license colleague, who can view it without ever paying for Pro.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about sharing a report in the Power BI service, per Chapter 9.
options: Sharing a report also shares access to its underlying semantic model by default
Hiding a table or column in a report prevents a recipient from ever seeing that data, even without row-level or object-level security
Build permission lets a recipient create their own new reports on top of the shared semantic model
Publish to web requires the same authentication as a normal share link
Reshare permission is off by default on every new sharing link
questions.explain: Sharing a report also shares access to its underlying semantic model — hiding a table or column is a clutter-reduction choice, not a security boundary, unless RLS or OLS actually restricts it. Build permission lets a recipient create new reports on the semantic model. Publish to web requires no authentication at all, which is exactly why it's never a substitute for ordinary sharing. Reshare is on by default, not off.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: only a workspace's ________ can delete it — and doing so permanently removes every dashboard, report, and semantic model inside, with no recovery.
questions.explain: Only a workspace's Admin can delete it, via Workspace settings. Deleting a workspace permanently removes every dashboard, report, semantic model, and dataflow inside it — there's no confirmation beyond one dialog, no recycle bin, no recovery.

questions.prompt: Match each Power BI service concept to what it actually is.
right: A collaborative container where a team's reports, models, and dashboards live together
The published, modeled version of your data — what used to be called a dataset
A single-page canvas of tiles pinned from one or more reports
A packaged, read-only bundle of reports, dashboards, and semantic models for a broad audience
questions.explain: A workspace is the collaborative container everything else lives in. A semantic model is the published, modeled version of your data. A dashboard is a single-page canvas of pinned tiles. An app is a packaged, read-only bundle of a workspace's content for a broader audience.

questions.prompt: A column is renamed in Desktop, but the file isn't republished. The next scheduled refresh in the service fails. Why, and what fixes it?
options: Data refresh only re-imports rows, never re-reads the source's structure; republishing from Desktop is required to pick up the renamed column
Scheduled refresh failures are always caused by an offline gateway, regardless of what changed
Renaming a column is reversible automatically the next time the gateway reconnects
The semantic model needs to be deleted and recreated from scratch any time a column is renamed
questions.explain: Data refresh in the service only re-imports rows — it never re-reads the source's table or column structure. A renamed column requires a schema refresh, which only happens in Desktop, followed by a republish, exactly as Lesson 70's republish mechanics describe.

questions.prompt: A scheduled refresh has now failed four times in a row. What happens next, automatically?
options: Power BI disables the schedule — it has to be fixed and manually switched back on
Power BI automatically switches the semantic model to DirectQuery mode
Nothing — Power BI keeps retrying indefinitely with no limit
The workspace is automatically removed from its assigned capacity
questions.explain: If a scheduled refresh fails four times in a row, Power BI automatically disables it, with no warning beyond the failure emails already sent. Re-enabling it requires fixing the underlying issue (often expired credentials), then flipping Schedule refresh's toggle back on.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: if no one opens any report or dashboard built on a semantic model for ________ months, Power BI automatically pauses its scheduled refresh and emails the owner.
questions.explain: After two full months with no one viewing any report or dashboard on a semantic model, Power BI automatically pauses its scheduled refresh, emails the owner, and marks the schedule Disabled. Any view, including through an app, resets the inactivity counter.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes what row-level security (RLS) restricts in Power BI?
options: RLS restricts which rows of data a user can see in a semantic model, filtered according to a role defined with a DAX expression
RLS restricts which specific columns or measures a user can see, while every row remains fully visible
RLS restricts which workspace roles (Admin, Member, Contributor, Viewer) a user can be assigned
RLS automatically hides entire report pages from users who aren't assigned to any role
RLS restricts how many scheduled refreshes a semantic model can run per day
RLS encrypts a semantic model's data so it can't be exported, regardless of which rows a user can see
questions.explain: RLS restricts which rows of data a user can see in a semantic model. You define the restriction as a role — a named DAX filter expression — in Desktop, then control who belongs to that role in the service. Every other column of a visible row still shows in full.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B describes object-level security (OLS), a separate feature that restricts columns and tables, not rows. RLS can never hide a column — if a user can see a row at all, they see every column of that row; restricting specific columns or measures requires OLS instead.

questions.prompt: A salesperson is assigned to an RLS role filtering them to only West region data, but they're also given the workspace Contributor role. What do they actually see?
options: Every region's data — RLS only restricts users assigned the workspace Viewer role; Contributors have edit permission and RLS never applies to them
Only West region data, since the RLS role always takes priority over workspace role
No data at all, since the two roles conflict and cancel each other out
West region data, but only in Desktop — the service ignores the role entirely for Contributors
questions.explain: RLS only restricts users assigned the workspace Viewer role. Workspace Admins, Members, and Contributors all have edit permission on the semantic model, and RLS never applies to them — regardless of which RLS role they might also be added to. To actually restrict someone, they must be a Viewer, nothing higher.

questions.prompt: A dynamic RLS role using this filter works correctly when tested in Desktop, but every assigned user sees zero rows once published to the service. What's the most likely cause?
options: The user-mapping table's email values don't match the UPN format USERPRINCIPALNAME() actually returns in the service
USERPRINCIPALNAME() only works inside Desktop and has no effect at all once published
Dynamic RLS roles are automatically disabled the moment a report is published
The role needs to be rebuilt using USERNAME() instead, since USERPRINCIPALNAME() is deprecated
questions.explain: The single most common dynamic RLS bug: the user-mapping table's values must match the format the function actually returns in the service, not necessarily what it showed while testing in Desktop. A mismatch between the mapping table's email format and the service's UPN format means no row ever matches, so every user sees nothing.

questions.prompt: The VP of Sales asks for "something that shows how we're doing." Per Lesson 84, what should a well-written requirement coming out of that conversation describe?
options: A decision the dashboard needs to support — like "which territories are ahead of or behind target" — not a chart type or color
The exact visual type and color scheme to use on each page
Every table and column available in AdventureWorksDW2014, regardless of whether it's needed
The specific DAX functions the measures should use
questions.explain: Requirements describe decisions, not visuals — the visuals come later, once the model exists to support them. "Which territories are ahead of or behind target" is a decision; a chart type or color choice is an implementation detail that belongs to a later lesson.

questions.code:
VAR ShippedOnTime =
    CALCULATE (
        COUNTROWS ( FactResellerSales ),
        USERELATIONSHIP ( FactResellerSales[ShipDateKey], DimDate[DateKey] ),
        FactResellerSales[ShipDateKey] <= FactResellerSales[DueDateKey]
    )
RETURN
    DIVIDE ( ShippedOnTime, COUNTROWS ( FactResellerSales ), 0 )
questions.prompt: Why does this fulfillment measure need USERELATIONSHIP specifically?
options: FactResellerSales has three date keys pointing at DimDate, but only the OrderDateKey relationship is active by default; USERELATIONSHIP activates the ShipDateKey relationship for just this one calculation
USERELATIONSHIP is required any time CALCULATE is used inside a VAR
DimDate was never related to FactResellerSales at all without this function
USERELATIONSHIP converts ShipDateKey from a whole number into a proper Date type
questions.explain: FactInternetSales and FactResellerSales both have multiple date keys pointing at DimDate (order, due, ship), but only one relationship can be active between two tables at a time — Power BI auto-activates OrderDateKey. USERELATIONSHIP activates the inactive ShipDateKey relationship for just this one measure, without disturbing every other measure's use of the active relationship.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the capstone's data model, per Lessons 87-88.
options: Two fact tables sharing dimension tables is still governed by star-schema modeling rules, sometimes called a galaxy schema
DimDate must be explicitly marked as a date table, since it relates to the fact tables through a whole-number surrogate key, not the date column itself
FactInternetSales can have all three of its date relationships (Order, Due, Ship) active at the same time
Only one relationship at a time can be active between FactInternetSales and DimDate, with the rest reachable via USERELATIONSHIP
A galaxy schema requires abandoning the cardinality and filter-direction rules learned for a single-fact-table star schema
questions.explain: Two fact tables sharing dimensions is still a star schema — sometimes called a galaxy schema — governed by the same modeling rules. DimDate needs explicit marking as a date table since the relationship runs through a surrogate key. Only one of FactInternetSales's three date relationships can be active at a time, with the other two reachable via USERELATIONSHIP — not all three active simultaneously, and nothing about a galaxy schema changes the underlying cardinality or filter-direction rules.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 84, well-written requirements describe ________ the dashboard needs to support, not chart types or colors.
questions.explain: Requirements describe decisions the dashboard needs to support — not visuals, chart types, or colors. Those implementation details come later, once the data model exists to support the actual decisions the requirements named.

questions.prompt: Match each capstone report page to what it's actually built to answer.
right: Which sales territories are ahead of or behind target
Which product categories drive margin, not just revenue
Whether reseller orders ship on time, and how this quarter compares to last year
A hidden drillthrough page showing product-level breakdown for one selected territory
questions.explain: Regional Performance answers which territories are ahead of or behind target. Product Profitability answers which categories drive margin. Fulfillment & Trend covers reseller on-time shipping plus the year-over-year comparison. Territory Detail is the hidden drillthrough page showing product-level detail for one selected territory, reached from Regional Performance.

questions.prompt: Put these stages of the capstone build process in the order Chapter 12 actually follows them.
items: Gather business requirements and write down the project's scope
Import the raw tables the scope identified, in Import mode
Clean and transform the data in Power Query
Build the star schema relationships in Model view
Write DAX measures, one per requirement
Build report pages and add interactivity
Publish, secure, and schedule refresh
questions.explain: The capstone follows the same order the whole course taught: requirements and scope first, then import, clean, model, measure, report, interact, and finally publish, secure, and refresh — each stage depending on the one before it, exactly like the five-step workflow from Chapter 1.

questions.code:
VAR CurrentSales = [Total Sales]
VAR PriorYearSales =
    CALCULATE ( [Total Sales], SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR ( DimDate[Date] ) )
RETURN
    DIVIDE ( CurrentSales - PriorYearSales, PriorYearSales, 0 )
questions.prompt: What does this measure calculate?
options: Year-over-year sales growth as a percentage, comparing the current period's sales against the same period one year prior
The running year-to-date total of sales
The percentage of total sales that occurred in the current year alone
A forecast of next year's sales based on the current trend
questions.explain: This is the variables-based year-over-year growth pattern: SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR shifts the date filter back one year to get PriorYearSales, and DIVIDE expresses the change from that prior value to the current one as a percentage — exactly the Chapter 5 variables style applied to the capstone's trend requirement.
